1.1: James a servant of God, and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve Tribes, which are scattered abroad, salutation.
1.2: My brethren, count it exceeding joy, when ye fall into divers tentations,
1.3: Knowing that ye trying of your faith bringeth forth patience,
1.4: And let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entier, lacking nothing.
1.5: If any of you lack wisedome, let him ask of God, which giveth to all men liberally, and reprocheth no man, and it shalbe given him.
1.6: But let him ask in faith, and wauer not: for hee that wavereth, is like a wave of the sea, tost of the wind, and caried away.
1.7: Neither let that man think that hee shall receive any thing of the Lord.
1.8: A double minded man is unstable in all his waies.
1.9: Let the brother of low degree reioyce in that he is exalted:
1.10: Again hee that is rich, in that hee is made low: for as the flower of the grass, shall he vanish away.
1.11: For as when the sunne riseth with heat, then the grass withereth, and his flower falleth away, and the goodly shape of it perisheth: even so shall the rich man wither away in all his waies.
1.12: Blessed is ye man, that endureth tentation: for when he is tried, hee shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him.
1.13: Let no man say when hee is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God can not bee tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man.
1.14: But every man is tempted, when hee is drawen away by his own concupiscence, and is entised.
1.15: Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth foorth sinne, and sinne when it is finished, bringeth foorth death.
1.17: Every good giving, and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variablenes, neither shadow of turning.
1.18: Of his own will begat hee us with the woorde of trueth, that we should be as the first fruites of his creatures.
1.19: Wherefore my dear brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath.
1.20: For the wrath of man doeth not accomplish the righteousness of God.
1.21: Wherefore lay apart all filthiness, and superfluitie of maliciousness, and receive with meekenes the word that is graffed in you, which is able to save your soules.
1.22: And be ye doers of the word, and not hearers onely, deceiving your own selves.
1.23: For if any hear the woorde, and doe it not, he is like unto a man, that beholdeth his natural face in a glass.
1.24: For when he hath considered himself, hee goeth his way, and forgetteth immediately what maner of one he was.
1.25: But who so looketh in the perfect Law of libertie, and continueth therein, hee not being a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the woorke, shalbe blessed in his deed.
1.26: If any man amog you seem religious, and refraineth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this mans religion is vain.
1.27: Pure religion and undefiled before God, even the Father, is this, to visit the fatherless, and widdowes in their aduersitie, and to keep himself unspotted of the world.

2.1: My brethren, have not the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ in respect of persons.
2.2: For if there come into your company a man with a gold ring, and in goodly apparell, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment,
2.3: And ye have a respect to him that weareth the gaie clothing; and say unto him, Sit thou here in a goodly place, and say unto the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footestoole,
2.4: Are yee not partial in your selves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?
2.5: Hearken my beloved brethren, hath not God chosen the poor of this world, that they should be rich in faith, and heires of the kingdom which he promised to them that love him?
2.6: But ye have despised the poor. Doe not the rich oppress you by tyrannie, and doe not they draw you before the iudgement seates?
2.7: Doe nor they blaspheme the worthie Name after which yee be named?
2.8: But if yee fulfil the royal Law according to the Scripture, which saith, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thy self, yee doe well.
2.9: But if yee regard the persons, yee commit sinne, and are rebuked of the Law, as transgressours.
2.10: For whosoever shall keep the whole Law, and yet faileth in one poynt, hee is guiltie of all.
2.11: For he that said, Thou shalt not commit adulterie, said also, Thou shalt not kill. Now though thou doest none adulterie, yet if thou killest, thou art a transgressour of the Law.
2.12: So speak ye, and so doe, as they that shall be judged by the Law of libertie.
2.13: For there shalbe condemnation merciles to him that sheweth not mercie, and mercie reioyceth against condemnation.
2.14: What availeth it, my brethren, though a man saith he hath faith, when he hath no workes? can that faith save him?
2.15: For if a brother or a sister bee naked and destitute of daily food,
2.16: And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace: warm your selves, and fil your bellies, notwithstading ye give them not those things which are needefull to the body, what helpeth it?
2.17: Even so the faith, if it have no woorkes, is dead in it self.
2.18: But some man might say, Thou hast the faith, and I have woorkes: shew me thy faith out of thy woorkes, and I will shew thee my faith by my woorkes.
2.19: Thou beleeuest that there is one God: thou doest well: the devils also beleeue it, and tremble.
2.20: But wilt thou understand, O thou vain man, that the faith which is without workes, is dead?
2.21: Was not Abraham our father justified through workes, when he offred Isaac his sonne upon the altar?
2.22: Seest thou not that the faith wrought with his workes? and through the workes was the faith made perfect.
2.23: And the Scripture was fulfilled which sayeth, Abraham beleeued God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and hee was called the friend of God.
2.24: Ye see then how that of workes a man is justified, and not of faith onely.
2.25: Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified through workes, when she had received ye messengers, and sent them out another way?
2.26: For as the body without ye spirit is dead, even so the faith without workes is dead.

3.1: My brethren, be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation.
3.2: For in many things we sinne all. If any man sinne not in word, he is a perfect man, and able to bridle all the body.
3.3: Behold, we put bittes into the horses mouthes, that they should obey us, and we turn about all their bodie.
3.4: Behold also the shippes, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce windes, yet are they turned about with a very small rudder, whither soever the gouernour listeth.
3.5: Even so the tongue is a litle member, and boasteth of great things: behold, how great a thing a litle fire kindleth.
3.6: And the tongue is fire, yea, a world of wickedness: so is the tongue set among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature, and it is set on fire of hell.
3.7: For the whole nature of beasts, and of birds, and of creeping things, and things of the sea is tamed, and hath been tamed of the nature of man.
3.8: But the tongue can no man tame. It is an unruly evil, full of deadly poyson.
3.9: Therewith bless we God even the Father, and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God.
3.10: Out of one mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing: my brethren, these things ought not so to be.
3.11: Doeth a fountain send forth at one place sweet water and bitter?
3.12: Can ye figge tree, my brethren, bring forth olives, either a vine figges? so can no fountain make both salt water and sweet.
3.13: Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? let him shew by good conversation his workes in meekenesse of wisdom.
3.14: But if ye have bitter envying and strife in your hearts, reioyce not, neither be liars against the trueth.
3.15: This wisedome descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, and devilish.
3.16: For where envying and strife is, there is sedition, and all maner of evil workes.
3.17: But the wisedome that is from above, is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easie to be intreated, full of mercie and good fruites, without judging, and without hipocrisie.
3.18: And the fruit of righteousness is sowen in peace, of them that make peace.

4.1: From whence are wars and contentions among you? are they not hence, even of your pleasures, that fight in your members?
4.2: Ye lust, and have not: ye enuie, and desire immoderately, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, and get nothing, because ye ask not.
4.3: Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye might lay the same out on your pleasures.
4.4: Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the amitie of the world is the enimitie of God? Whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world, maketh himself the enemie of God.
4.5: Doe ye think that the Scripture sayeth in vain, The spirit that dwelleth in us, lusteth after enuie?
4.6: But the Scripture offereth more grace, and therefore sayth, God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
4.7: Submit your selves to God: resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
4.8: Draw neere to God, and he will draw neere to you. Clense your handes, ye sinners, and purge your hearts, ye double minded.
4.9: Suffer afflictions, and sorrow ye, and weep: let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into heaviness.
4.10: Cast down your selves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.
4.11: Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, or he that condemneth his brother, speaketh evil of ye Law, and condemneth the Law: and if thou condemnest the Law, thou art not an observer of the Law, but a judge.
4.12: There is one Lawgiver, which is able to save, and to destroy. Who art thou that judgest another man?
4.13: Goe to now ye that say, To day or to morowe we will goe into such a citie, and continue there a yeere, and bye and sell, and get gain,
4.14: (And yet ye cannot tell what shalbe to morowe. For what is your life? It is even a vapour that appeareth for a litle time, and afterward vanisheth away)
4.15: For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, and, if we live, we will doe this or that.
4.16: But now ye reioyce in your boastings: all such reioycing is evil.
4.17: Therefore, to him that knoweth how to doe well, and doeth it not, to him it is sinne.

5.1: Goe to now, ye rich men: weep, and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you.
5.2: Your riches are corrupt, and your garments are moth eaten.
5.3: Your gold and silver is cankred, and the rust of them shalbe a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh, as it were fire. Ye have heaped up treasure for the last dayes.
5.4: Behold, the hire of ye labourers, which have reaped your fieldes (which is of you kept back by fraud) cryeth, and the cryes of them which have reaped, are entred into the eares of the Lord of hostes.
5.5: Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and in wantonnes. Ye have nourished your heartes, as in a day of slaughter.
5.6: Ye have condemned and have killed the just, and he hath not resisted you.
5.7: Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman wayteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the former, and the latter rayne.
5.8: Be ye also patient therefore and settle your hearts: for ye coming of the Lord draweth neere.
5.9: Grudge not one against another, brethren, least ye be condemned: behold, the judge standeth before the door.
5.10: Take, my brethren, the Prophets for an ensample of suffering aduersitie, and of long patience, which have spoken in the Name of the Lord.
5.11: Behold, we count them blessed which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have knowen what end the Lord made. For the Lord is very pitiful and merciful.
5.12: But before all thinges, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by any other othe: but let your yea, be yea, and your nay, nay, lest ye fall into condemnation.
5.13: Is any among you afflicted? Let him pray. Is any merie? Let him sing.
5.14: Is any sick among you? Let him call for the Elders of the Church, and let them pray for him, and anoynt him with oyle in the Name of the Lord.
5.15: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up: and if he have committed sinnes, they shalbe forgiven him.
5.16: Acknowledge your faultes one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed: for the prayer of a righteous man availeth much, if it be fervent.
5.17: Helias was a man subiect to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rayne, and it rayned not on the earth for three yeeres and six moneths.
5.18: And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rayne, and the earth brought forth her fruit.
5.19: Brethren, if any of you hath erred from the trueth, and some man hath converted him,
5.20: Let him know that he which hath converted the sinner from going astray out of his way, shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sinnes.

59:1:1: That is, written to no one man, city or country, but to all the Jews generally, being now dispersed.
To all the believing Jews, of what Tribe soever they be, and are dispersed through the whole world.
59:1:2: The first place or part touching comfort in afflictions, wherein we ought not be cast down and be fainthearted, but rather rejoice and be glad.
Seeing their condition was miserable in that scattering abroad, he doth well to begin as he doth.
The first argument, because our faith is tried through afflictions: which ought to be most pure, for so it is behoovable for us.
59:1:3: The second, Because patience, far passing and most excellent virtue, is by this means engendered in us.
That wherewith your faith is tried, to wit, those manifold temptations.
59:1:4: The third argument propounded in manner of an exhortation, that true and continual patience may be discerned from fained and for a time. The cross is as it were the instrument wherewith God doth polish and [re]fine us. Therefore the work and effect of afflictions, is the perfecting of us in Christ.
59:1:5: By wisdom he meaneth the knowledge of that doctrine whereof mention was made before, to wit, wherefore we are afflicted of God, and what fruit we have to reap of affliction.

An answer to a privy objection: It is easily said, but it is not so easily done. He answereth that we need in this case a far other manner of wisdom, than the wisdom of man, to judge those things best for us, which are most contrary to the flesh: but yet we shall easily obtain this gift of wisdom, if we ask it rightly, that is, with a sure confidence of God, who is most bountiful and liberal.
59:1:6: A digression or going aside from his matter, against prayers which are conceived with a doubting mind, whereas we have a certain promise of God, and this is that second part of the Epistle.
Why then what need other Mediator?
59:1:8: In all his thoughts and his deeds.
59:1:9: Who is afflicted with poverty, or contempt, or with any kind of calamity.
He returneth to his purpose, repeating the proposition, which is, that we must rejoice in the cross, for it doth not press us down, but exalt us.
59:1:10: An argument taken of the very nature of the things themselves, for that they are most vain and uncertain.

Before he concludeth, he giveth a doctrine contrary to the former: to wit, how we ought to use prosperity, which is plenty of all things: to wit, so that no man therefore please himself, but be so much the more void of pride.
Who hath all things at his will.
59:1:11: Whatsoever he either purposeth in his mind, or doeth.
59:1:12: The conclusion: Therefore we must patiently bear the cross: and he addeth a fourth argument, which comprehendeth the sum of all the former, to wit, because we come by this way to the crown of life, but yet of grace according to the promise.
Affliction whereby the Lord trieth him.
59:1:13: Here is a reason showed, why God cannot be the author of evil doing in us, because he desireth not evil.

The third part of this Epistle, wherein he descendeth from outward tentations, that is, from afflictions, whereby God trieth us, to inward, that is, to those lusts whereby we are stirred up to do evil. The sum is this: Every man is the author of these temptations to himself, and not God: for we bear about in our bosoms that wicked corruption, which taketh occasions by what means soever, to stir up evil motions in us, whence out at length proceed wicked doing, and in conclusion followeth death the just reward of them.
When he is provoked to do evil.
59:1:15: By sin is meant in this place actual sin.
59:1:16: Another reason taken of contraries: God is the author of all goodness, and so, that he is always like himself; how then can he be thought to be author of evil?
59:1:17: From him who is the fountain and author of all goodness.
He goeth on in the metaphor: for the sun by his manifold and sundry kinds of turning, maketh hours, days, months, years, light and darkness.
59:1:18: The fourth part concerning the excellency and fruit of the word of God. The sum is this: we must hear the word of God most carefully and diligently, seeing it is the seed, wherewith God of his free favor and love hath begotten us unto himself, picking us out of the number of his creatures. And the Apostle condemneth two faults, which do greatly trouble us in this matter, to wit, for that we so please ourselves, that we had rather speak ourselves than hear God speaking: yea, we snuff and are angry when we are reprehended: against which faults, he setteth a peaceable and quiet mind, and such an one as is desirous of purity.
This is it which Paul calleth gracious favor, and good will, which is the fountain of our salvation.
As it were an holy kind of offering, taken out of the residue of man.
59:1:21: By meekness, he meaneth modesty, and whatsoever is contrary to an haughty and proud stomach.
59:1:22: Another admonition. Therefore is God’s word heard, that we may frame our lives according to the prescript thereof.
He addeth reasons, and those most weighty: first, because they that do otherwise, do very much hurt themselves.
59:1:23: He alludeth to that natural spot, to which is contrary that purity whereunto we are born again, the lively image whereof we behold in the Law.
Secondly, because they lose the chiefest use of God’s word, which correct not by it the faults that they know.
59:1:25: Behaving himself so: for works do show faith.
59:1:26: The fountain of all brabbling, and cursed speaking, and sauciness, is this, that men know not themselves.
The third admonition: The word of God prescribeth a rule not only to do well, but also to speak well.
59:1:27: The fourth: the true service of God standeth in charity toward our neighbors (especially such as need others’ help, as the fatherless and widows), and purity of life.
To have a care of them, and to help them as much as we can.
59:2:1: The fifth: Charity which proceedeth from a true faith, cannot stand with the accepting of persons: which he proveth plainly by setting forth their example, who with the reproach or disdain of the poor, honor the rich.
For if we knew what Christ’s glory is, and esteemed it as we ought to do, there would not be such respect of persons as there is.
59:2:3: In a worshipful and honorable place.
59:2:4: Have ye not (which you ought not to do) by this means with yourselves judged one man to be preferred before another?
59:2:5: He showeth that they are perverse and naughty Judges, which prefer the rich before the poor, by that that God on the contrary side preferreth the poor, whom he hath enriched with true riches, before the rich.
The needy and wretched, and (if we measure it after the opinion of the world) the veriest abjects of all men.
59:2:6: Secondly, he proveth them to be mad men: for that the rich men are rather to be holden execrable and cursed, considering that they persecute the Church, and blaspheme Christ: for he speaketh of wicked and profane rich men, such as the most part of them have been always, against whom he setteth the poor and abject.
59:2:7: Word for word, which is called upon of you.
59:2:8: The Law is said to be royal and like the King’s highway, for that it is plain and without turnings, and that the Law calleth everyone our neighbor, without respect, whom we may help by any kind of duty.
The conclusion: Charity which God prescribeth cannot agree with the accepting of persons, seeing that we must walk in the King’s highway.
59:2:10: A new argument to prove the same conclusion: They do not love their neighbors, which neglect some, and ambitiously honor others: for he doth not obey God, which cutteth off from the commandments of God that that is not so commodious for him, nay he is rather guilty generally for the breach of the whole Law, although he observe the residue.
Not that all sins are equal, but because he that breaketh one tittle of the Law, offendeth the majesty of the Lawgiver.
59:2:11: A proof: because the Lawmaker is always one and the selfsame, and the body of the Law cannot be divided.
59:2:12: The conclusion of the whole treatise: we are upon this condition delivered from the curse of the Law by the mercy of God, that in like sort we should maintain and cherish charity and goodwill one towards another, and whoso doth not so, shall not taste of the grace of God.
59:2:13: He that is hard and currish against his neighbor, or else helpeth him not, he shall find God an hard and rough Judge to himselfward.
59:2:14: The fifth place which hangeth very well with the former treatise, touching a true and lively faith. And the proposition of this place is this: faith which bringeth not forth works, is not that faith whereby we are justified, but an image of faith: or else this, they are not justified by faith, which show not the effects of faith.
59:2:15: The first reason taken of a similitude: If a man say to one that is hungry, Fill thy belly, and yet giveth him nothing, this shall not be true charity: so if a man say he believeth, and bringeth forth no works of his faith, this shall not be a true faith, but a certain dead thing set out with the name of faith, whereof no man hath to brag, unless he will openly incur reprehension, seeing that the cause is understood by the effects.
59:2:18: Nay, thus may every man beat down the pride.
59:2:19: Another reason taken of an absurdity: If such a faith were the true faith whereby we are justified, the devils should be justified: for they have that, but yet notwithstanding they tremble, and are not justified therefore, neither is that faith a true faith.
59:2:20: The third reason from the example of Abraham, who no doubt had a true faith: but he in offering his son, showed himself to have that faith which was not void of works, and therefore he received a true testimony when it was said, that faith was imputed to him for righteousness.
59:2:21: Was he not by his works known and found to be justified? for he speaketh not here of the causes of justification, but by what effects we may know that a man is justified.
59:2:22: That the faith was declared to be a true faith, and that by works.
Was effectual and fruitful with good works.
59:2:23: Then was the Scripture fulfilled, when it appeared plainly, how truly it was written of Abraham.
59:2:24: The conclusion: he is only justified that hath that faith which hath works following it.
Of that dead and fruitless faith which you boast of.
59:2:25: A fourth reason taken from a like example of Rahab the harlot, who also proved by her works that she was justified by a true faith.
59:2:26: The conclusion repeated again: faith which bringeth not forth fruits and works, is not faith, but a dead carcass.
59:3:1: Unless we surcease from this masterlike and proud finding fault with others.
The sixth part or place: Let no man usurp (as most men ambitiously do) authority to judge and censure others righteously.
A reason: Because they provoke God’s severity against themselves, which do so curiously and rigorously condemn others, being themselves guilty and faulty.
59:3:2: The seventh place, touching the bridling of the tongue, joined with the former, so that it is manifest that there is no man which may not justly be found fault withal, seeing it is a rare virtue to bridle the tongue.
59:3:3: He showeth by two similitudes the one taken from the bridles of horses, the other from the rudders of ships, how great matters may be brought to pass by the good moderation of the tongue.
59:3:5: On the contrary part he showeth how great discommodities arise by the intemperance of the tongue, throughout the whole world, to the end that men may so much the more diligently give themselves to moderate it.
59:3:6: It is able to set the whole world on fire.
59:3:9: Amongst other faults of the tongue, the Apostle chiefly reproveth backbiting and speaking evil of our neighbors, even in them especially which otherwise will seem godly and religious.

He denieth by two reasons, that God can be praised by that man, that useth cursed speaking, or to backbite: first because man is the image of God, which whosoever reverenceth not doth not honor God himself.
59:3:10: Secondly, because the order of nature which God hath set in things, will not suffer things that are so contrary the one to the other, to stand the one with the other.
59:3:13: The eighth part which hangeth with the former, touching meekness of mind, against which he setteth envy and a contentious mind. And in the beginning he stoppeth the mouth of the chief fountain of all these mischiefs, to wit, a false persuasion of wisdom, whereas notwithstanding there is no true wisdom, but that is heavenly, and frameth our minds to all kinds of true moderation and simplicity.
59:3:17: He setteth mercy against the fierce and cruel nature of man, and showeth that heavenly wisdom bringeth forth good fruits, for he that is heavenly wise, referreth all things to God’s glory, and the profit of his neighbor.
59:3:18: Because the world persuadeth itself that they are miserable which live peaceably and simply, on the contrary side the Apostle pronounceth that they shall at the length reap the harvest of peaceable righteousness.
59:4:1: He goeth on forward in the same argument, condemning certain other causes of wars and contentions, to wit, unbridled pleasures and immoderate lusts, by their effects, for so much as the Lord doth worthily make them void, so that they bring nothing else to them in whom they are but incurable torments.
59:4:2: He reprehendeth them by name, which are not ashamed to go about to make God the minister and helper of their lusts and pleasures, in asking things which either are of themselves unlawful, or being lawful, ask them to wicked purposes and uses.
59:4:4: Another reason why such unbridled lusts and pleasures are utterly to be condemned, to wit, because that he that giveth himself to the world, divorceth himself from God, and breaketh the band of that holy and spiritual marriage.
59:4:5: The taking away of an objection: Indeed our minds run headlong into these vices, but we ought so much the more diligently take heed of them: which care and study shall not be in vain, seeing that God resists the stubborn, and giveth that grace to the modest and humble that surmounteth all those vices.
59:4:7: The conclusion: We must set the contrary virtues against those vices, and therefore whereas we obeyed the suggestions of the devil, we must submit our minds to God, and resist the devil, with a certain and assured hope of victory: To be short, we must employ ourselves to come near unto God by purity and sincerity of life.
59:4:9: By this word the Greeks meant an heaviness joined with shamefastness, which is to be seen in a cast down countenance, and settled as it were upon the ground.
He goeth on in the same comparison of contraries, and setteth against those profane joys with an earnest sorrow of mind, and against pride and arrogance, holy modesty.
59:4:11: He reprehended most sharply another double mischief of pride: the one is in that the proud and arrogant will have other men to live according to their will and pleasure and therefore they do most arrogantly condemn whatsoever pleaseth them not: which thing cannot be done without great injury to our only Lawmaker, for by this means his Laws are found fault withal, as not circumspectly enough written, and men challenge that unto themselves which properly belongeth to God alone, in that they lay a Law upon men’s consciences.
59:4:13: The other fault is this: that men do so confidently determine upon these and those matters and businesses, as though that every moment of their life did not depend of God.
59:4:17: The conclusion of all the former treatise: The knowledge of the will of God doth not only nothing at all profit, unless the life be answerable unto it, but also maketh the sins far more grievous.
59:5:1: He denounceth utter destruction to the wicked and profane rich men, and such as are drowned in their riotousness, mocking at their foolish confidence when as there is nothing indeed more vain than such things.
59:5:4: The Lord who is more mighty than ye are, hath heard them.
59:5:5: The Hebrews call a day that is appointed to solemn banqueting, a day of slaughter or feasting.
59:5:7: He applieth that to the poor, which he spake against the rich, warning them to wait for the Lord’s coming patiently, who will revenge the injuries which the rich men do them.

The taking away of an objection: Although his coming serve to linger, yet at the least we must follow the husbandmen, who do patiently wait for the times that are proper for the fruits of the earth. And again, God will not defer the least iota of the time that he hath appointed.
59:5:9: He commendeth Christian patience, so that whereas others through impatience use to accuse one another, the faithful on the contrary side complain not, although they receive injury.
By grudging, he meaneth a certain inward complaining which betokeneth impatience.
The conclusion: The Lord is at the door, who will defend his own, and revenge his enemies, and therefore we need not to trouble ourselves.
59:5:10: Because most men are wont to object, that it is good to repel injuries by what means soever, he setteth against that, the examples of the Fathers, whose patience had a most happy end, because God as a most bountiful Father, never forsaketh his.
59:5:12: Because even the best men sometimes through impatience break out into oaths sometimes lesser, sometimes greater, the Apostle warneth us to detest such wickedness, and to accustom our tongues to simple and true talk.
That that you have to say or affirm, speak or affirm it simply, and without an oath: and that that you will deny, deny it simply and flatly.
59:5:13: He showeth the best remedy against all afflictions, to wit, prayers which have their place both in sorrow and joy.
59:5:14: He showeth peculiarly, to what physicians especially we must go, when we are diseased, to wit, to the prayers of the Elders, which then also could cure the body, (for so much as the gift of healing was then in force) and take away the chiefest cause of sickness and diseases, by obtaining for the sick through their prayers and exhortations, remission of sins.
This was a sign of the gift of healing: and now seeing we have the gift no more, the sign is no longer necessary.
By calling on the Name of the Lord.
59:5:15: He hath reason in making mention of sins, for diseases are for the most part sent because of sins.
59:5:16: He commendeth prayers by the effects that come of them, that all men may understand that there is nothing more effectual than they are, so that they proceed from a pure mind.

Because God pardoneth their sins which confess and acknowledge them, and not theirs which justify themselves, therefore the Apostle addeth, that we ought freely to confer one with another touching those inward diseases, that we may help one another with our prayers.
59:5:19: Hath called him back from his way.

The taking away of an objection: All reprehensions are not condemned, seeing that on the contrary part there is nothing more acceptable to God, than to call into the way a brother that was wandering out of the way.
